row.description: Tally is Simbe’s autonomous retail shelf-auditing robot family, first publicly introduced on November 10, 2015, when the announcement described retailer trials. Current 4.0-era marketing states up to 12 h per charge, over a dozen high-resolution cameras, turn-in-place navigation and robot localization within 1–2 in in a 150,000 sq ft store. These current claims are not inherited by all historical generations or RFID configurations. The original 2015 release described approximately 30 lb and a 38 in base/adjustable mast design; those dated figures are not current outer dimensions or mass. Shelf observations feed software tasks and dashboards. Current RaaS prices require a quote, and supplier certification/fleet claims retain their dates and scope.
row.navigationAccuracy: Current family page claims robot localization within 1–2 in in a 150,000 sq ft store; test conditions unspecified
row.driveMode: Current family page: autonomous aisle traversal, path planning, obstacle avoidance and turn-in-place navigation

highlights: Autonomous aisle and shelf scanning
Identifies stock gaps, misplaced products and price-label errors
Connects findings to staff task lists and store dashboards

The November 10, 2015 manufacturer release explicitly introduces Tally as its first product and says it is in retailer trials. Its approximately 30 lb mass and 38 in height with adjustable mast belong to that historical design; no exact current mass/dimensions or automatic equivalence to named Tally 1.0 is established.

The current page describes up to 12 hours of operation per charge, faster charging without an exact duration, path planning/obstacle avoidance and turn-in-place navigation. These are 4.0-era family-page claims, not universal specifications for Tally 1.0, 2.0, 2.6, 3.0 or every RFID installation.

The current page claims localization within 1–2 inches in a 150,000 sq ft store and 99% shelf-label identification using over a dozen high-resolution cameras. Localization, label-recognition percentage and RFID read range are distinct measurements; independent test conditions and dimensional vision precision are not supplied.

The timeline distinguishes Tally 1.0 internal deployment in 2016, Tally 2.0 customer deployment in 2017, Tally RFID launch in 2018, Tally 2.6 introduction in 2019, Tally 3.0 launch in 2020 and Tally 4.0 launch separately dated January 12, 2026. Deployment years do not establish exact first release dates.

The March 4, 2026 manufacturer announcement reports UL 3300 certification for Tally and its charging dock; no independent listing or coverage of every historical revision is verified. The September 21, 2026 fleet announcement says 3,000 autonomous units under contract, not 3,000 delivered robots or independently proven market leadership.

highlights: ER-FLEX 250-7e combines a MiR250 mobile base with the Universal Robots UR7e arm. The integration sheet gives 7.5 kg arm payload and 850 mm reach excluding the tool; the model suffix is not an exact load or reach specification.

Sim2Real-based stack planning supports mixed cases without prior item-specific programming, and configurable SKU-based patterns are described. row.description: Tally RFID is the named RFID-enabled Tally sensing configuration, announced on July 18, 2018 as integration of RFID and machine learning with computer vision. The current product page claims up to 120,000 items in 3 h and up to 750 tag reads/s. It gives conflicting range text: headline up to 35 ft and body up to 40 ft; the configuration or test basis is unresolved. RFID reading distance is not navigation accuracy or a guaranteed all-item detection radius. The 2018 release’s over-700-tags/s and sub-meter product-location claims retain their historical scope. RAIN/GS1 standards wording is an attributed supplier claim. Current Tally 4.0 battery/mass and fixed-camera Tally Spot specifications are not inherited.
row.driveMode: Autonomous retail inventory traversal with combined computer vision and UHF RFID sensing; base-chassis revision unspecified
row.throughput: Supplier claims up to 120,000 items in 3 h and up to 750 tag reads/s; item counts and raw read-event rate differ, test layout unspecified

highlights: Named RFID-equipped configuration of the Tally autonomous retail inventory robot
Combines UHF RFID sensing with computer vision to track tagged merchandise
Inventory dashboards help store teams identify misplaced stock and follow inventory changes

The July 18, 2018 manufacturer announcement explicitly introduces RFID/ML integration alongside Tally’s existing computer vision. It calls the result Tally RFID and describes scale deployments, while a retained availability paragraph also says trials. This establishes the dated capability launch, not a universal transaction or stock status.

The current RFID page claims up to 120,000 items scanned in three hours and up to 750 tag reads per second. Counted inventory items and raw read events are different quantities; neither implies every item/tag/store always meets the stated maximum.

The same current page says up to 35 ft read range in its headline and up to 40 ft in its body; the current Tally family page also uses up to 40 ft. The unresolved RFID range text is retained explicitly, without choosing a presumed corrected value or placing range in navigation accuracy.

The 2018 launch reports over 700 RFID tags/s and sub-meter location of merchandise. Those dated supplier claims do not establish current robot pose accuracy or replace the current page’s 750-tags/s claim. RAIN Alliance–GS1 UHF Gen2 wording is supplier-reported standards positioning, not an independently checked certificate.

Tally RFID names a sensing configuration, without proving a separately redesigned drive base. The current Tally page’s up-to-12-hour battery rating is not transferred to every RFID configuration; fixed-camera Tally Spot, mobile software, dashboards and ROI estimates are separate system roles.

highlights: Diana 7 combines seven torque-sensing axes with 7 kg payload and 923 mm working radius. The brochure lists 28 kg robot mass separately from a 16 kg control box; neither controller mass nor cabinet dimensions are the arm envelope.

row.description: K3 is the indoor autonomous security robot documented in Knightscope’s 2023 Form 10-K. The filing lists approximately 340 lb, 4 ft height and 2 ft width, with geofenced navigation using lasers, ultrasonic sensors, an IMU and wheel encoders. Its K3/K5 family statement gives roughly 2–3 hours patrol and charging stops of about 20 minutes or more. K3 disables the parking-utilization, parking-meter and plate-recognition functions described for K5. Current availability and first-release year remain unestablished.
row.chargingTime: Approximately 20 minutes or more per charging stop (2023 family statement; not full recharge)

highlights: The 2023 Form 10-K explicitly names K3 as an indoor ASR, approximately 4 ft high, 2 ft wide and 340 lb. These are historical named-model specifications; the missing guessed product page and omission from the current Force page do not alone prove discontinuation.

K3/K5 navigation in the filing combines lasers, ultrasonic sensors, an inertial measurement unit and wheel encoders for geofenced patrol and scheduled routes. It is manufacturer-described operation, not proof of universal obstacle avoidance or independent safety certification.

The 2023 family statement gives approximately 2–3 hours of patrol before an autonomous charging stop of about 20 minutes or more. Monitoring remains operational while charging; advertised 24/7 service is not 24 hours of travel on one charge and the stop is not a proven empty-to-full recharge.

The filing says K3 shares the anomaly-detection suite described for K5, but parking utilization, parking-meter and license-plate-recognition features are turned off. Outdoor plate-recognition marketing is therefore not transferred to this indoor configuration.

Browser-based KSOC, intercom and public-address functions in the historical filing retain their product-generation scope. The current Signals/ASF architecture, future network plans and human guarding services are not automatically confirmed upgrades on every legacy K3.

row.handType: Intelligent multi-suction parcel gripper; modular robotic induction cells
row.description: AmbiSort B-Series is Ambi Robotics’ modular induction and sorting system, introduced June 6, 2023. Robot arms use multi-suction parcel grasping, a central conveyor and six-sided scanning to route to configured containers or exception outputs. The launch claims over 1,200 parcels/h, while the linked 2023 guide’s specification footnote states a three-induction-cell configuration. The current configurator says each pick cell adds 500 sorts/h; this is not a universal one-cell or complete-line guarantee. The launch’s over 99.5% accuracy and guide’s different accuracy/sortability contexts remain supplier claims, not dimensional vision precision. Input, outputs, arm count and layout are configuration choices; operators replenish full containers.

The launch states throughput exceeding 1,200 parcels/h. Those configuration and date contexts remain separate rather than turning 1,200/h into a single-arm guarantee or deriving an exact linear whole-system rate.

An intelligent multi-suction gripper singulates parcels from deep bins or conveyors, followed by a buffer/central conveyor and a six-sided scan tunnel. A/B series remain separate named systems: A-Series uses four barcode scanners and two QC zones in its described sack workflow; B-Series uses six-sided scan-tunnel induction and configurable gaylord/other outputs. AmbiOS/AmbiAccess and 24/7 support are software/service roles; no current numeric complete-system purchase or RaaS price is established.

row.description: Sanbot commercial service-robot family with Professional, Standard and Economic configurations. The matrix distinguishes powered navigation hardware from a manually pushed Economic base and gives different mass and battery specifications. row.description: Pool cleaner combining JetPulse twin-jet surface skimming with floor, wall and waterline cleaning. SonicSense ultrasonic sensing supports obstacle and depth-transition detection. Surface parking and drainage assist retrieval. February 2026 specifications give mode-dependent endurance; 6 L debris capacity and up-to-3230 sq ft pool coverage are storage and per-charge coverage, not payload or hourly throughput.

highlights: JetPulse twin jets guide floating debris toward the inlet; SonicSense uses ultrasonic sensing for obstacles, slopes and platform transitions. The stated 8-inch shallow-water limit retains its model-specific scope.
